note: The datasheet library: every source of data the explainer computes from or quotes, and sources worth adding. Status is not stored here; src/scripts/library.js works it out from usedBy at build time. A use without `pr` must be cited (its `find` text present) in that file on this tree, or `npm run check` fails. `reuse` is what the source states about copying (open, cite, unknown); `license` gives the detail, read on the `checked` date. Links only: no PDFs are rehosted.

sources.title: CIE 1931 colour-matching functions, 2 degree observer
sources.edition: data set from CIE 018:2019, Table 6; DOI 10.25039/CIE.DS.xvudnb9b
sources.provides: The standard observer at 1 nm: how strongly the eye's three color channels respond to each wavelength. Every color on the site is an integral against these curves.
sources.license: CIE publishes its data sets under CC BY-SA 4.0 (read from the CIE D65 data set's metadata; share-alike means derived tables carry the same license).

sources.title: Simple Analytic Approximations to the CIE XYZ Color Matching Functions
sources.by: Chris Wyman, Peter-Pike Sloan and Peter Shirley
sources.provides: A sum of piecewise Gaussians that reproduces the CIE 1931 curves to about 1%, so the engine needs no table.
sources.license: Authors keep copyright; JCGT articles may be redistributed unmodified under CC BY-ND 4.0 and their code is under an open-source license. The fit's coefficients are copied into optics-core.js with this citation.

sources.title: CIE standard illuminant D65, illuminant A, typical fluorescent lamps (FL11) and typical LED lamps (LED-B3)
sources.provides: Spectral power of daylight, tungsten, a tri-phosphor tube and a white LED, the lamps on the lamp switch. D65 doi 10.25039/CIE.DS.hjfjmt59; FLs 10.25039/CIE.DS.ukaymjdn; LEDs 10.25039/CIE.DS.vgssnyfg.
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (stated in the D65 data set's metadata). The tables in lamps.json are copies, so they carry CC BY-SA.

sources.title: Colour (colour-science)
sources.provides: A Python colour-science library whose copies of the CIE tables were used to build lamps.json, and the CIE 1964 10° table, Stockman & Sharpe fundamentals and CIE 2015 functions behind observers.json.
sources.license: BSD 3-Clause.

sources.title: Optical spectroscopic study of tetrahedrally coordinated Co²⁺ in natural spinel and staurolite at different temperatures and pressures
sources.provides: Measured absorption of tetrahedral Co²⁺ and the assignment of its triplet, the ⁴A₂ → ⁴T₁(P) transition that makes cobalt blue. The page cites it for the physics; the curve itself is the measured glass of Meulebroeck et al. 2016.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated (the PDF is restricted).

sources.title: Glasses for Protecting the Eyes from Injurious Radiations
sources.by: W. W. Coblentz and W. B. Emerson, Bureau of Standards
sources.edition: Technologic Paper 93; the free copy is the 3rd edition, 1919
sources.provides: Measured ultraviolet, visible and infrared transmission of protective glasses, including ferrous heat-absorbing glass. Sets the strength of the Fe²⁺ infrared band on the glory-hole lenses.
sources.license: US government work; no license stated on the document.

sources.title: The CIEDE2000 color-difference formula: implementation notes, supplementary test data, and mathematical observations
sources.by: Gaurav Sharma, Wencheng Wu and Edul N. Dalal
sources.provides: The color-difference formula and test data the rack's recipe fits are scored with.
sources.license: Journal article; formula used with citation.

sources.title: A Low-Dimensional Function Space for Efficient Spectral Upsampling
sources.provides: The three-number sigmoid spectrum used to relight photographed swatches under other lamps.
sources.license: Journal article; method used with citation.

sources.title: Bullseye Glass Co. online store
sources.edition: swept for the rack (328 colors, COE 90)
sources.provides: Names, codes and product photos of Bullseye sheet, frit, rod and billet. Rack swatches are sampled from the photos; colorants are inferred from names.
sources.license: No data license stated. The repo keeps names, codes, links and one sampled color per product, not the photos.

sources.title: Glass Alchemy online store
sources.provides: Names and product photos of Glass Alchemy borosilicate color rod. Swatches sampled from photos.
sources.license: No data license stated. Names, links and sampled colors only.

sources.title: Frantz Art Glass online store
sources.by: Frantz Art Glass (a Perle di Vetro company)
sources.edition: swept for Effetre, Reichenbach, CiM, Vetrofond, Double Helix, Northstar and TAG
sources.provides: Catalog codes, names and photos for seven lampwork rod brands a retailer resells. Swatches sampled from photos.
sources.license: No data license stated. Names, codes, links and sampled colors only.

sources.title: Craig Johnson's LED Museum: fluorescence spectra of a uranium glass marble
sources.provides: Spectrograph plots of a uranium glass marble and a uranium glass insulator fluorescing under a 445 nm laser module. uranium.js places uranium glass's strongest emission peak near 527 nm from the marble's plot, read by eye.
sources.license: No copyright or terms notice on the page. Plots are images; no numbers are copied beyond the peak position.
sources.caution: The 527 nm peak is read by eye from a plotted image; the page gives no numbers. A related page (eighth/blu-ray.htm) shows the same kind of glass under a Blu-ray laser, about 405 nm.

sources.title: Viscosity of a standard soda-lime-silica glass
sources.by: Albert Napolitano and Earl G. Hawkins, National Bureau of Standards
sources.provides: Viscosity of NBS Standard Glass No. 710 from 560 to 1400 °C, measured at eight laboratories, with a Fulcher fit and the strain (504 °C), annealing (546 °C) and softening (724 °C) points.
sources.license: US government publication; no license stated. Fit constants and fixed points are quoted with citation.

sources.title: ATS-129: Properties of Soda-Lime Silica Float Glass
sources.edition: technical bulletin, current edition dated 09/2026; PR #16 cites the 2013-01-14 edition
sources.provides: Elastic, thermal and optical constants of float glass: E = 72 GPa, expansion 8.3 × 10⁻⁶ /°C, density, conductivity, heat capacity, and a rule for reading stress from optical retardation.
sources.license: Disclaimer only; no reuse license stated.
sources.caution: The 2026 edition gives Poisson's ratio 0.22; the stage uses 0.23 from the 2013 edition and says so (about a 1% difference in stress).

sources.title: The annealing of glass; and A Note on the Annealing of Optical Glass
sources.by: L. H. Adams and E. D. Williamson
sources.provides: Measurements of how stress decays in hot glass, the basis of annealing schedules, and their law that the rate of relief goes as the square of the stress, dσ/dt = −Aσ².
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: Do cathedral glasses flow?
sources.provides: The shear modulus (about 30 GPa) and viscosity extrapolation that turn room-temperature glass into a relaxation time longer than the age of the universe.
sources.license: Journal article (AIP); no reuse license stated. The site now links the DOI.

sources.title: Viscous flow of medieval cathedral glass
sources.by: Ozgur Gulbiten, John C. Mauro, Xiaoju Guo and Olus N. Boratav
sources.provides: Room-temperature viscosity of a medieval Westminster Abbey glass, estimated from its composition (10²⁴–10²⁵ Pa·s) and flow of about 1 nm per billion years.
sources.license: Journal article (Wiley); no reuse license stated.

sources.title: SCHOTT optical glass datasheets (N-BK7, F2, SF11, N-SF11)
sources.edition: values as in the SCHOTT Zemax catalog 2017-01-20b; the downloads page gives no version for the current collection
sources.provides: Sellmeier coefficients, refractive index nd and Abbe number vd for each glass, plus internal transmittance and thermal data. The downloads page also offers the catalog in Zemax format.
sources.license: No terms of use on the downloads page. The repo takes the coefficients through the CC0 refractiveindex.info copy, and links SCHOTT for the datasheet itself.

sources.title: refractiveindex.info database
sources.provides: Optical constants of thousands of materials as YAML, including the SCHOTT, Ohara and Hoya catalogs. The source of every Sellmeier coefficient the site uses, and of the Johnson & Christy and Rioux metal constants behind the struck colors.
sources.license: CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication).

sources.title: Interspecimen Comparison of the Refractive Index of Fused Silica
sources.provides: The standard Sellmeier fit for fused silica, 0.21 to 3.71 µm.
sources.license: Journal article; coefficients quoted with citation.

sources.title: Optical properties of soda lime silica glasses
sources.provides: Refractive index and absorption of window glass from the ultraviolet to the infrared; the page's soda-lime index curve.
sources.license: Journal article (Elsevier); coefficients quoted with citation.

sources.title: Council Directive 69/493/EEC on the approximation of the laws of the Member States relating to crystal glass
sources.provides: Legal definitions of lead crystal (at least 24% PbO) and full lead crystal (at least 30%), with density and refractive-index limits.
sources.license: EU legislation; quoted with citation (EUR-Lex reuse terms not re-read).

sources.title: An investigation of the origin of the colour of the Lycurgus Cup by analytical transmission electron microscopy
sources.by: D. J. Barber and I. C. Freestone
sources.provides: Analytical TEM of the Lycurgus Cup glass: the color comes from silver-gold alloy nanoparticles.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: The Lycurgus Cup — A Roman nanotechnology
sources.by: Ian Freestone, Nigel Meeks, Margaret Sax and Catherine Higgitt
sources.provides: About 40 ppm gold and 300 ppm silver in the cup; particles 50–100 nm, about 7:3 silver to gold with some copper; only a handful of other Roman dichroic pieces; routine gold ruby from 17th-century Europe. Also summarizes Brill's 1960s analyses (VII Int. Congress on Glass, Brussels 1965, paper 223, not seen directly).
sources.license: Journal article (Springer, open access); no reuse license checked.

sources.title: Formation of gold nanoparticles in gold ruby glass: the influence of tin
sources.by: S. Haslbeck, K.-P. Martinek, L. Stievano and F. E. Wagner
sources.provides: Gold ruby glasses with 200 ppm gold and up to 2 wt% tin, struck around 600 °C: tin gives many small particles, and color runs from purple-red (little tin) to brown (much tin).
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: Optical constants of the noble metals
sources.by: P. B. Johnson and R. W. Christy
sources.provides: Measured n and k of copper, silver and gold films from 0.5 to 6.5 eV. The page's struck gold, silver and copper colors are computed from these, through Mie theory.
sources.license: The article is cited; the tabulated values are copied from the refractiveindex.info database (CC0).

sources.title: An analytic model for the dielectric function of Au, Ag, and their alloys
sources.by: D. Rioux, S. Vallières, S. Besner, P. Muñoz, E. Mazur and M. Meunier
sources.provides: A model fitted to ellipsometry of gold, silver and three alloy films, tabulated for any composition. The Lycurgus Cup's particles are modeled with its 30% gold, 70% silver alloy.
sources.license: The article is cited; the tabulated alloy values come from the refractiveindex.info database (CC0).

sources.title: Beiträge zur Optik trüber Medien, speziell kolloidaler Metallösungen
sources.provides: The exact solution of Maxwell's equations for a sphere, worked out to explain the colors of colloidal gold.
sources.license: Public domain by age.

sources.title: Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles
sources.by: Craig F. Bohren and Donald R. Huffman
sources.provides: Mie theory and the BHMIE algorithm (appendix A) that mie.js follows: logarithmic derivative by downward recurrence, Riccati–Bessel functions by upward recurrence, efficiencies and asymmetry parameter.
sources.license: Book; the method is reimplemented, no code copied.

sources.title: Optical Properties of Metal Clusters
sources.provides: The surface-scattering correction γ(r) = γ_bulk + A·v_F / r for electrons in small metal particles, and the spread of reported A values.
sources.license: Book; the formula is used, no text or data copied.

sources.title: miepython: Mie scattering of light by perfect spheres
sources.provides: Reference values the tests check mie.js against (efficiencies, backscatter, asymmetry).
sources.license: MIT. Only numbers it computed are in the tests; no code copied.

sources.title: Electron–electron and electron-hole interactions in small semiconductor crystallites: the size dependence of the lowest excited electronic state
sources.provides: The effective-mass estimate of how a semiconductor crystal's band gap rises as it shrinks, used for the selenium ruby striking slider.
sources.license: Journal article; the formula is used.

sources.title: Glass Dictionary: gold ruby; lead glass; and the exhibition Glass of the Alchemists: lead crystal and gold ruby, 1650–1750
sources.provides: Kunckel perfected gold ruby at Potsdam shortly before 1679 and made it at the Elector's glassworks with purple of Cassius by the mid-1680s; Glauber is also credited with the purple; Ravenscroft patented his glass in 1674 and added more lead in 1676.
sources.license: Museum web pages; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: Quantum size effect in three-dimensional microscopic semiconductor crystals
sources.by: A. I. Ekimov and A. A. Onushchenko
sources.provides: The first report of quantum confinement in semiconductor nanocrystals: copper chloride crystals in glass, whose absorption shifts blue as they shrink.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2023: press release and popular information
sources.by: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
sources.provides: Ekimov at the S. I. Vavilov State Optical Institute, copper chloride in glass heated at 500–700 °C for 1 to 96 hours, and the prize shared with Brus and Bawendi.
sources.license: Nobel Prize outreach pages; no reuse license checked.

sources.title: On the communication of the structure of doubly refracting crystals to glass, muriate of soda, fluor spar, and other substances, by mechanical compression and dilatation
sources.provides: The discovery that stressed or unevenly heated glass becomes birefringent.
sources.license: Published 1816; public domain.

sources.title: Glass Stress—Optical Coefficient (C770); Polariscopic Examination of Glass Containers (C148); Measuring Optical Retardation and Analyzing Stress in Glass (F218)
sources.provides: How the stress-optic coefficient of a glass is measured, and polariscope practice; C148 specifies a sensitive tint plate of nominal 565 nm retardation.
sources.license: Paid standards; cited, not copied.

sources.title: The atomic arrangement in glass
sources.provides: The continuous random network picture of oxide glass and the rules an oxide must obey to form one.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: Direct imaging of a two-dimensional silica glass on graphene
sources.provides: Atom-by-atom electron micrographs of a bilayer silica glass, the first direct image of a Zachariasen network.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: Computer generation of structural models of amorphous Si and Ge
sources.by: F. Wooten, K. Winer and D. Weaire
sources.provides: Building a random network from a crystal by bond switches and relaxation; stage 00's drawing sketches the method.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, vol. I, ch. 31: The Origin of the Refractive Index
sources.by: R. P. Feynman, R. B. Leighton and M. Sands
sources.provides: The driven-oscillator derivation of the refractive index, and why it rises toward an absorption resonance.
sources.license: Free to read online; copyright Caltech; no reuse license.

sources.title: Opticks: or, a Treatise of the Reflections, Refractions, Inflections and Colours of Light
sources.edition: 1st edition 1704; the online copy is the 4th edition, 1730 (Project Gutenberg eBook 33504)
sources.provides: Newton's experiments on refraction and color, including his view that dispersion goes with refraction.
sources.license: Public domain.

sources.title: On the coefficient of viscous traction and its relation to that of viscosity
sources.provides: Extensional viscosity is three times the shear viscosity, measured on pitch and other very viscous liquids.
sources.license: Published 1906; public domain.

sources.title: The viscous catenary
sources.provides: States the Stokes–Rayleigh analogy between slow viscous flow and incompressible elasticity, crediting Stokes (1845) and Rayleigh's Theory of Sound.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.
sources.caution: Journal volume and pages not yet confirmed.

sources.title: Under what conditions can a glass be formed?
sources.provides: Glass formation as a race between cooling and crystal nucleation and growth.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: Formation of monatomic metallic glasses through ultrafast liquid quenching
sources.by: L. Zhong, J. Wang, H. Sheng, Z. Zhang and S. X. Mao
sources.provides: Pure refractory metals such as tantalum made glassy in nanometer volumes by quenching at about 10¹⁴ K/s (rate and metal confirmed from the PubMed abstract).
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: Theory of two-dimensional melting; Two-step melting in two dimensions: first-order liquid-hexatic transition
sources.by: B. I. Halperin and D. R. Nelson; E. P. Bernard and W. Krauth
sources.provides: The hexatic phase between a two-dimensional crystal and liquid: predicted in 1978, shown for hard disks in 2011.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: Force fields for silicas and aluminophosphates based on ab initio calculations
sources.by: B. W. H. van Beest, G. J. Kramer and R. A. van Santen
sources.provides: The charged pair potential most often used to simulate silica glass.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: Confusion by design; Stabilization of metallic supercooled liquid and bulk amorphous alloys; A highly processable metallic glass
sources.by: A. L. Greer; A. Inoue; A. Peker and W. L. Johnson
sources.provides: The confusion principle, Inoue's empirical rules for bulk metallic glasses (three or more elements), and the five-element Vitreloy 1.
sources.license: Journal article; no reuse license stated.
sources.caution: Inoue's three-element rule is quoted from the paper's well-known summary; the passage was not re-read on the checked date.

sources.title: Authenticity screening of stained glass windows using optical spectroscopy
sources.by: Wendy Meulebroeck, Hilde Wouters, Karin Nys and Hugo Thienpont
sources.provides: Measured 300–1500 nm transmission of 85 panes of two stained-glass panels, plotted as absorbance in arbitrary units (each curve normalized 0..1; no thickness given): cobalt blues (Fig. 2), chromium greens with Cr³⁺ and Cr⁶⁺ (Fig. 3), iron yellows (Fig. 4), copper-ruby flashes (Fig. 5) and silver stain (Fig. 8). The page traces B1 (cobalt), G1 (chromium) and SY2 (silver) from the figures for their shapes.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0. The traced curves in measured.json are an adaptation, credited there and here.

sources.title: Optical investigation and electronic polarizability of Nd³⁺ doped soda-lime-silicate glasses
sources.by: P. Chimalawong, J. Kaewkhao and P. Limsuwan
sources.provides: Absorption of (65−x)SiO₂·25Na₂O·10CaO·xNd₂O₃ glasses (x = 0–5 mol%), 3 mm thick, 300–700 nm (Fig. 3), with the Nd³⁺ bands assigned: 4G5/2+2G7/2 at 583 nm, 4G7/2+4G9/2+2K13/2 near 525 nm, 4F9/2 near 680 nm. The page traces x = 1, 2 and 3 for neodymium's shape, which turns the glass blue-gray under the fluorescent tube.
sources.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on the article page). The traced curve in measured.json is an adaptation, credited there and here.

sources.title: Mathematical description of absorbance spectra for Fe and Cu doped soda-lime-silica glasses
sources.edition: PhD thesis, University of Sheffield (White Rose eTheses 6086)
sources.provides: Gaussian bands fitted to measured absorbance of 15Na₂O·15CaO·70SiO₂ glasses doped with iron and copper, 1 cm thick, reflection and host-glass losses removed, with heights in absorbance per cm per mol% of the ion (Tables 5.4.1–5.4.3, 6.6.2). The page's Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺ and Cu²⁺ curves are these bands, so their amounts are real.
sources.license: Thesis; the repository record states no reuse license. The page copies 17 fitted numbers (band positions, widths and heights) with this citation, not text or figures.

sources.title: Color in commercial glasses
sources.edition: IMI-NFG Glass Processing Course, lecture 4, spring 2015 (slides, Lehigh University)
sources.provides: Iron in commercial glass: three weak Fe³⁺ ligand-field bands at 385, 420 and 435 nm, the strongest just outside the visible, whose tail removes blue-violet and leaves oxidized glass yellow-green; one Fe²⁺ band at 1050 nm. A second source for the hue the site computes from Volotinen's bands; it does not list Volotinen's fainter green and red bands.
sources.license: Course slides, NSF-sponsored (DMR-0844014); no reuse license stated.

sources.title: SCHOTT optical filter glass data sheets and calculation program
sources.edition: data sheets version June 2026 (169 pp); Excel calculation program with 2015 tutorial
sources.provides: Measured internal transmittance of colored glasses, 200–5200 nm, at a reference thickness: cobalt blues (BG), coppers, ferrous heat absorbers (KG), selenium–cadmium long-pass reds and oranges (RG, OG), neutral densities (NG). The Excel tool rescales to any thickness.
sources.would: Industrial colored glass measured to datasheet standard, to check each drawn colorant curve and the Beer–Lambert thickness scaling against.
sources.license: No reuse license stated; values are "reference values". Use to check curves and quote individual numbers with citation, not to copy tables.

sources.title: SciGlass
sources.by: EPAM Systems (open release); SciGlass Next at Universität Jena
sources.edition: v1.0 MS Access release (May 2019), read through D. R. Cassar's plain-text conversion (github.com/drcassar/SciGlass, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.8287159); browsable as SciGlass Next at sciglass.uni-jena.de (API by key on request)
sources.provides: About 422,000 glass compositions with their properties (viscosity, transition temperature, expansion, index) and over 15,000 optical spectra, ultraviolet to near infrared. The bench uses 10,257 melts made only of its nine oxides, with measured viscosity points, index and Abbe number, extracted by tools/sciglass/extract.py. Its room-temperature density model is fitted to 7,452 of SciGlass's measured densities (tools/sciglass/fit_density.py), and its alumina–magnesia viscosity correction to 2,971 of the melts (tools/sciglass/fit_viscosity.mjs).
sources.would: Measured spectra for uranium and didymium glass (the spectra are not in the open text conversion; SciGlass Next shows them).
sources.license: ODbL per SciGlass Next; the GitHub LICENSE file is headed ODbL but its body is the MIT license. Treat as ODbL (attribution and share-alike), the stricter reading: the extract public/data/sciglass/bench.json carries the ODbL notice and is offered under ODbL 1.0.
sources.caution: A compilation of literature values, not a curated reference: duplicates and mistyped entries exist (one entry at NBS 710's composition lists n = 1.618). Fluegel's viscosity model was fitted to much of the same literature, so agreement with it is a consistency check, not independent validation.

sources.title: TIE-29: Refractive Index and Dispersion
sources.provides: How SCHOTT defines and fits index: the Sellmeier form, Abbe numbers, partial dispersions and tolerances.
sources.would: A citable check on the cut stage's formulas and its Abbe-number definitions.
sources.license: No reuse license stated.

sources.title: TIE-35: Transmittance of optical glass
sources.edition: current PDF undated; earlier version October 2005
sources.provides: Internal versus external transmittance, surface reflection losses and how to rescale transmittance to another thickness.
sources.license: No reuse license stated.
sources.caution: Gives the reflection factor P from Fresnel's formula (0.92 at n ≈ 1.5) rather than a flat 4% a face, and notes that thick high-index glasses often look yellowish.

sources.title: NIST Atomic Spectra Database (Standard Reference Database 78)
sources.by: A. Kramida, Yu. Ralchenko, J. Reader and the NIST ASD Team
sources.provides: Evaluated atomic lines. Sodium D2 588.995095 nm and D1 589.592424 nm in air, matching the values in flare.js.
sources.license: NIST Standard Reference Data can be copyrighted under the Standard Reference Data Act; no license text found. Quote values with the recommended citation.

sources.title: Standard Reference Material 710a: Soda-Lime-Silica Glass
sources.by: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.provides: Certified viscosity from log η = 2 (1464 °C) to 5 (918 °C) poise and a certified softening point of 730.6 °C, with annealing 545 °C and strain 504 °C for information. A different melt from NBS 710 (zinc and alumina added).
sources.would: A second, certified soda-lime curve to show how much fixed points move between two similar glasses.
sources.license: US government certificate; no license stated.

sources.title: TechNotes 4: Heat & Glass, and the Annealing Thick Slabs chart
sources.provides: A studio glass maker's annealing soak (482 °C) and cooling rates by thickness, derived from Corning's method, and how kiln glass behaves at each temperature.
sources.would: Real studio schedules for the lehr, in place of float-glass numbers applied to studio glass.
sources.license: © Bullseye Glass Co.; no reuse license stated.

sources.title: Colour & Vision Research Laboratory database
sources.by: Institute of Ophthalmology, University College London
sources.provides: Tabulated color-matching functions (CIE 1931, Stiles–Burch, CIE 2006), cone fundamentals and luminous efficiency.
sources.would: Tables to test the analytic observer against, and a second copy of the CIE 2006 tables to check observers.json against (cvrl.org did not answer from the build container on 2026-10-19, so the tables came through asano-2016).
sources.license: "Provided free of charge as a service to the vision science community"; no explicit reuse license.

sources.title: CIE 1964 colour-matching functions, 10 degree observer
sources.edition: data set from ISO/CIE 11664-1:2019, Table 2; DOI 10.25039/CIE.DS.sqksu2n5
sources.provides: The standard observer for fields about 10° across: the wide-field eye of the many-observers stage.
sources.license: CIE open-access data set. Its page shows no license text and its metadata file was not read, so the CC BY-SA 4.0 read from the D65 set is assumed here, not checked.

sources.title: Fundamental Chromaticity Diagram with Physiological Axes, Part 1
sources.provides: Cone fundamentals built from their parts: photopigment absorbance, pigment density by field size, macular pigment, and lens density by age (the Pokorny, Smith & Lutze 1987 formula). Gives an eye of any age from 20 to 80 and any field from 2° to 10°.
sources.license: Paid CIE publication. The model is cited; its tables reached the repo through Asano et al.'s distribution (asano-2016).

sources.title: Fundamental Chromaticity Diagram with Physiological Axes, Part 2
sources.provides: The linear map from cone fundamentals to cone-based XYZ functions, 2° and 10°. observers.json refits it from colour-science's tables (residual about 1e-6).
sources.license: Paid CIE publication; only the nine matrix coefficients are used, refitted from open tables.

sources.title: Individual Colorimetric Observer Model
sources.by: Yuta Asano, Mark D. Fairchild and Laurent Blondé
sources.provides: An individual-observer extension of CIE 2006. Its distribution carries the CIE 170-1 component tables at 5 nm that observers.json holds, copied from the luxpy package (v1.12.5) data folder.
sources.license: Article CC BY 4.0 (PLoS ONE). The tables are CIE 170-1 values; luxpy's code is GPL-3.0, and none of it is copied, only the numbers.

sources.title: Computerized simulation of color appearance for dichromats
sources.by: Hans Brettel, Françoise Viénot and John D. Mollon
sources.provides: How a dichromat's colors look to a trichromat: two half-planes in cone space through white, anchored at 475 and 575 nm (protan, deutan) or 485 and 660 nm (tritan).
sources.license: Journal article (Optica); the method is cited and reimplemented, nothing copied.

sources.title: Loci of achromatic points throughout the life span
sources.by: John S. Werner and Brooke E. Schefrin
sources.provides: Fifty observers aged 11 to 78: the white point does not shift significantly with age. The support for treating every eye as adapted to its own lens.
sources.license: Journal article (Optica); the finding is cited.

sources.title: Glass viscosity calculation based on a global statistical modelling approach
sources.by: Alexander Fluegel, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory
sources.edition: Glass Technol.: Eur. J. Glass Sci. Technol. A 48(1), 13–30; author's copy on glassproperties.com
sources.provides: Isokom temperatures at 10^1.5, 10^6.6 and 10^12 Pa·s as polynomials in mol% composition, fitted to more than 2,200 silicate glasses (about 42–89 mol% SiO2), with the paper's own predictions for standard glasses (Table 12).
sources.license: Journal article, author's copy; no reuse license stated. Coefficients are quoted with citation.
sources.caution: Coefficients are as printed in the PDF's text layer (read again 2026-10-20, JBK-1002); with them the bench reproduces Table 12 for all five standards within 0.5 °C. An earlier machine reading had the CaO term at 10^1.5 wrong (−16.843, a neighbouring cell, for −17.453) and three entries unreadable. The bench adds an Al2O3×MgO correction of its own, fitted to SciGlass (JBK-1011); it is labelled as not Fluegel's.

sources.title: Density and thermal expansion calculation of silicate glass melts from 1000 °C to 1400 °C
sources.by: Alexander Fluegel, David A. Earl, Arun K. Varshneya and Thomas P. Seward III, Alfred University
sources.edition: Phys. Chem. Glasses: Eur. J. Glass Sci. Technol. B 49(5); author's copy on glassproperties.com
sources.provides: Melt density at 1000–1400 °C as a function of mol% composition (Table 2), fitted to SciGlass data for glasses above 40 mol% silica.
sources.license: Journal article, author's copy; no reuse license stated. Coefficients are quoted with citation.
sources.would: Melt density at working temperatures, should a stage need the hot glass's weight. The bench used it for room-temperature density until JBK-1003 (scaled to 2.50 g/cm³ for float glass, it ran a median 0.05 g/cm³ light) and now uses a SciGlass fit instead.
sources.caution: A melt model, not a room-temperature one.

sources.title: Older thermal expansion models (Appen's factors, as tabulated)
sources.by: Alexander Fluegel, after A. A. Appen, Glass Chemistry (1974)
sources.provides: Appen's additive factors for the linear expansion coefficient by mol%, including the composition-dependent rules for SiO2, B2O3, PbO and K2O. The page traces additive expansion factors back to Winkelmann and Schott (1894).
sources.license: No terms stated on the site. Factors are quoted with citation.

sources.by: John C. Young and Alfred N. Finn, National Bureau of Standards

sources.license: US government publication; no license stated. Factors are quoted with citation.
